question: Assume today is 2026-08-23. You know nothing published after this date. Estimate the number of live births in South Korea in July 2026, as it will be first reported in the national statistics agency's monthly Population Trends release.

target.what: Number of live births occurring in South Korea during July 2026, as first reported in the national statistics agency's monthly Population Trends release (population trend / vital statistics).
target.cadence: monthly, typically released about two months after the reference month
target.caveats: The target is a flow of live births by month of occurrence, not by month of registration. The first report for July 2026 would normally be published around late September 2026, after the information cutoff of 2026-08-23. The July 2026 period is completed relative to the cutoff, but the official figu

candidates.hypothesis: The number of live births in July 2026 can be estimated by extrapolating the recent trend and seasonal pattern from the most recent monthly birth counts published before the cutoff. July typically has a seasonal factor relative to adjacent months.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly live birth counts for South Korea from January 2023 through June 2026 (or the latest available month before 2026-08-23), including the same month in previous years (July 2023, July 2024, July 2025) and recent year-over-year changes. Minimum evidence: a time series of at least 24 months of monthly births and the latest 3–6 months of year-over-year growth rates.

candidates.perspective: Resident registration births and administrative records
candidates.hypothesis: Monthly counts of birth registrations from the resident registration system (주민등록) can serve as a leading or coincident indicator for the vital statistics live birth count, after adjusting for registration lag and coverage differences.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly number of birth registrations in South Korea from January 2024 through July 2026 (or latest available), ideally from Ministry of the Interior and Safety (행정안전부) resident registration data. Also find the historical ratio of vital-statistics live births to resident-registration births for the same months to calibrate the bridge.
search_hints: resident registration births South Korea monthly 2026

candidates.perspective: Hospital and health insurance birth claims
candidates.hypothesis: National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) or Health Insurance Review & Assessment Service (HIRA) data on childbirth-related claims can provide a near-real-time proxy for monthly births, with a stable ratio to the vital statistics count.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly counts of childbirth-related medical claims or delivery cases from NHIS/HIRA for 2024–2026, and the historical ratio of these claims to official live births. Minimum evidence: at least 12 months of overlapping data to estimate the conversion factor.
search_hints: NHIS childbirth claims monthly South Korea

candidates.perspective: Demographic accounting from population and fertility rates
candidates.hypothesis: Live births in July 2026 can be approximated by multiplying the estimated mid-2026 female population aged 20–39 by an age-specific fertility rate for July, adjusted for seasonality. This route requires population estimates and recent fertility rates.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly or quarterly female population by age (especially 20–39) for 2026 from Statistics Korea, and recent age-specific fertility rates or total fertility rate (TFR) with monthly seasonality. Minimum evidence: mid-2026 female population 20–39 and a recent TFR or age-specific rates.

candidates.perspective: Policy and calendar effects on births
candidates.hypothesis: Recent policy changes (e.g., parental benefits, housing support) or calendar effects (e.g., Lunar New Year timing, marriage trends) may have shifted the number of births in July 2026 relative to the historical trend. Quantifying these effects can adjust the extrapolation.
candidates.data_to_find: Evidence on major birth-related policy changes implemented in 2025–2026, monthly marriage registrations (as a leading indicator of births with a lag), and any known calendar effects. Minimum evidence: a list of relevant policies with implementation dates and monthly marriage counts for 2025–2026.

candidates.hypothesis: Statistics Korea or other institutions may have published monthly or quarterly birth projections for 2026 that can serve as a prior for July 2026, though these are forecasts rather than realized outcomes.
candidates.data_to_find: Any published monthly or quarterly birth projections for 2026 from Statistics Korea, Bank of Korea, or research institutes, with methodology notes. Minimum evidence: a projection for 2026 total births or a monthly path.

assessment.note: Same sentence, same measurement (May 2026 births level and its YoY change); p2 is the ratio form of p1. Not independent evidence, but jointly they pin the May 2026 level at 23,160 and the May 2025 base at 20,379.
Two outlets reporting the same KOSTAT January–May 2026 cumulative growth of 15.2%. Same underlying statistic, so this is one observation, not two.
May 2026 TFR of 0.85 and its +0.10 YoY change appear in both the Segye and eToday reports; same KOSTAT release, single underlying measurement.

Monthly TFR path for Jan–May 2026 from one article: 0.99, 0.93, 0.93, 0.93, 0.85. Internally consistent and consistent with p4/p5; useful for judging whether the May dip is seasonal or a break in trend.

May 2026 marriages down 1,392 (-6.4%) YoY; level and rate from the same sentence. Relevant as a leading indicator for births roughly 9–15 months later, i.e. mostly beyond July 2026, so it constrains the trend direction rather than the July level.
Natural decrease of 6,413 in May 2026 implies deaths of 29,573; consistent with the birth level in p1 and useful only as a coherence check on the same release.

NHIS/HIRA-type delivery-case counts for 2024–2025 (national total plus Sejong, Gyeongbuk, Jeju). They corroborate the direction of the 2025–2026 birth upturn and give a level anchor for 2025, but they are annual, regionally partial, and measured on a different basis (delivery claims, not registered live births), so they cannot be substituted directly for a July 2026 monthly vital-statistics count.

2025 annual TFR of 0.80 versus the 2026 monthly TFRs of 0.85–0.99 shows the 2026 upturn is real and large; it also warns that monthly TFRs are noisy and seasonally shaped, so the May 0.85 should not be read as a collapse.

methods.rationale: Route: July 2026 births = July 2025 births x the 2026 YoY factor. The July 2025 base is not directly observed, so it is proxied by the May 2026 level (p1, 23,160) divided by the May 2026 YoY factor implied by p1's own change (13.6%), which recovers the May 2025 base; the assumption a1 then carries the July 2026 YoY factor. This is a deliberate transfer: it assumes the May 2025-to-July 2025 level change is small relative to the 2026 upturn, and that the 2026 YoY factor observed through May applies to July. Failure modes: the May 2026 level is a single noisy month; the May-to-July seasonal step is ignored; and the 2026 upturn could fade. The wide a1 range is the main uncertainty carrier.

Route: use the January–May 2026 cumulative level (p3, 122,694 births) as the best-observed 2026 birth level, convert it to a monthly average by dividing by the five months covered, then apply the July seasonal factor a2. This is a level-based cross-check on m1 and uses a different observed input (the cumulative total rather than the May month). Failure modes: the January–May average may not represent the second half of 2026 if the upturn is decelerating (p6 marriages, p4 TFR dip); the seasonal factor a2 is an assumption, not a kept observation; and the cumulative figure is subject to the same KOSTAT revision risk as p1.

assumptions.name: July 2026 live births relative to July 2025 live births
assumptions.rationale: The only kept evidence on the 2026 birth trajectory is the January–May cumulative growth of 15.2% (p3) and the May 2026 YoY increase of 13.6% (p1). July 2026 is a completed period whose births were largely conceived in late 2025, so the 2026 upturn should still be present, but the May marriage decline of 6.4% (p6) and the May TFR dip to 0.85 (p4) argue for some moderation. A central factor of 1.13 with a wide 1.05–1.22 range brackets a continuation of the ~14–15% pace and a slowdown toward high single digits.
assumptions.applies_when: Used to scale a July 2025 live-birth base to July 2026; valid only if the 2026 upturn observed through May persists into July and no new shock (policy, epidemic, calendar) intervenes.
assumptions.falsified_by: A June 2026 KOSTAT release showing YoY growth below about 5% or above about 20%, or evidence that the May 2026 upturn was a registration-timing artifact rather than a real increase in births.

assumptions.name: July seasonal factor relative to the annual average monthly birth level
assumptions.rationale: Korean monthly births show a mild seasonal pattern, with July typically slightly below the annual monthly average because of the autumn-conception peak. This factor is needed to convert an annual or January–May-based level into a July-specific level; it is a dimensionless seasonal adjustment, not a restatement of the target level.
assumptions.applies_when: Used to adjust a 2026 annual or cumulative birth level to the July 2026 month; valid if the historical July seasonal shape is stable in 2026.
assumptions.falsified_by: A published KOSTAT monthly seasonal-adjustment table showing July 2026 deviating materially from the historical July factor, or a June 2026 release implying a different within-year shape.

Same May 2026 marriage statistic (20,368 cases, -1,392, -6.4%); one measurement, two expressions. Marriages are a leading indicator for births roughly 9-15 months later, so May 2026 marriages bear mainly on 2027 births, not July 2026.

All from one NHIS/HIRA-based delivery-case article: national 2025 deliveries 252,000 (+6.1% vs 237,484 in 2024), with regional detail. They share one underlying measurement system and one publication, so they corroborate each other only weakly; they are useful as an annual-level cross-check on the direction and size of the 2025-2026 birth rebound.

Delivery cases +6.1% in 2025 and live births +15.2% in Jan-May 2026 point the same way (a rebound), but they cover different periods and different measurement systems (claims vs vital statistics), so the magnitudes are not directly comparable.

Natural decrease of 6,413 in May 2026 implies deaths of 29,573; combined with p1's 23,160 births this is internally consistent with the same release and confirms the birth level, but adds no independent information on July.

methods.rationale: Anchors on the May 2026 YoY increase in live births (p1 = 2,781 persons) and scales it by the assumed July 2026 YoY change factor a1. Because p1 is an increment, the product gives the July 2026 increment over July 2025; combined with the implied July 2025 base this yields the July 2026 level. Shared dependency: both the May increment and the July factor come from the same KOSTAT release lineage, so a revision to the May figure moves the whole estimate. Main failure mode: the YoY increment is not stable month to month, and July 2026 is two months beyond the last observation.

Uses the cumulative Jan-May 2026 live-birth growth rate (p3 = 15.2%) as a proxy for the 2026 level relative to 2025, converts the cumulative growth into a monthly-scale factor by dividing by the number of months in the year, and applies the July seasonal index a2 to place July relative to the annual average month. This route is deliberately coarse: it treats the Jan-May growth rate as representative of the full year and relies on a seasonal factor that is not directly observed in the kept points. Shared dependency with m1: both rest on the same KOSTAT 2026 release. Main failure mode: the Jan-May growth rate may not persist, and the seasonal index is an assumption rather than a measured coefficient.

assumptions.name: July 2026 live births relative to July 2025 live births
assumptions.rationale: The only pre-cutoff KOSTAT evidence on the 2026 birth level is the May 2026 YoY increase of 13.6% (p1/p2) and the Jan-May cumulative increase of 15.2% (p3). July 2026 is two months beyond the last observed month, so the YoY factor is centered slightly below the May figure to allow for mean reversion and for the fact that the 2025 base itself was rising through the year; the P10-P90 range spans a continuation of the rebound at a slower pace up to a near-repeat of the May jump. This is a change factor, not a level of the target.
assumptions.applies_when: The 2026 birth rebound observed through May continues into July at a somewhat attenuated pace, and no new shock (e.g., a policy change or a sharp marriage decline) intervenes between May and July 2026.
assumptions.falsified_by: A June 2026 KOSTAT release showing YoY growth falling to near zero or turning negative, or a documented break in the registration/occurrence relationship for mid-2026.

assumptions.name: July seasonal index relative to the annual average month
assumptions.rationale: Korean monthly births show a mild seasonal pattern with July typically slightly below the annual average month (autumn and winter months are higher). The value is a dimensionless seasonal factor applied to an annualized level; it is not a level of the target and is not supplied by any kept point.
assumptions.applies_when: The historical July seasonal pattern of Korean live births remains broadly stable in 2026.
assumptions.falsified_by: Evidence that the 2026 monthly seasonal profile has shifted materially (e.g., a documented change in conception timing or in the registration-to-occurrence lag).

The interval is [[p10]] to [[p90]], a model-based range conditional on the assumptions rather than a demonstrated accuracy guarantee.

The estimate rests on one method ([[n_methods]] method, weight [[m1_weight]]). It anchors on the observed May 2026 year-over-year increase and scales it by an assumed July 2026 year-over-year factor of [[a1_value]] (range [[a1_low]] to [[a1_high]]). The best computed estimate for live births occurring in South Korea during July 2026, as first reported by Statistics Korea's monthly Population Trends release, is 3,154 persons. The interval is 2,135 to 4,660, a model-based range conditional on the assumptions rather than a demonstrated accuracy guarantee.

The estimate rests on one method (1 method, weight 100%). It anchors on the observed May 2026 year-over-year increase and scales it by an assumed July 2026 year-over-year factor of 1.13 (range 0.7997 to 1.599). The May increment is observed; the July factor is an analyst assumption, centered below the May figure to allow mean reversion.

The main risk is that this assumed factor is wrong, since July 2026 lies beyond the last observed month. The most useful missing evidence would be June 2026 or early-July registration data, which could replace the assumption with observation.

Key assumptions (proposed by the analyst model, not observed; code samples each one between the bounds shown):
- a1 July 2026 live births relative to July 2025 live births: 1.13 ratio, range 0.7997 to 1.599 (range widened by code); used by m1. Overturned by: A June 2026 KOSTAT release showing YoY growth falling to near zero or turning negative, or a documented break in the registration/occurrence relationship for mid-2026.

by_construction: Only URLs leave the searcher (code regex); extractor, judge and final prompts never contain search result titles, snippets or the searcher's text. This holds by construction and is not measured.
residual_risks: The searcher sees post-cutoff search results and chooses which URLs are fetched, so page selection can be conditioned on the answer; only the URLs leave the searcher, and in backtests every fetched page is a snapshot dated <= as_of.
Live pages are used only when as_of is today; in backtests every page is an archived snapshot dated <= as_of.
The leak sentinel only catches registered official values in common formats, not paraphrased or derived numbers.
The model's own training data (knowledge cutoff unpublished) can include history before as_of; it cannot include the target if the target was published after the model's release.
Wayback snapshots are captured by a third party; a snapshot date <= as_of proves the content existed by then.
Assumption values are proposed by the judge model from its own knowledge, which can include the target's history before as_of; code checks their form, not where the number came from.
